title: Fixed Income
topic: Fixed income markets, trading, risk, and the life of a bond position — fixed income as a business and operating system, following the full life of a trade from investment idea through execution, settlement, funding, risk measurement, P&L attribution, and controls

concepts.title: Fixed Income Is a Business of Cash Flows
concepts.brief: Build the foundational mental model: fixed income is the business of pricing, financing, hedging, and managing contractual or modeled cash flows. Cover: what fixed income means and why 'fixed' income is not always fixed; lending and borrowing through securities; the players (issuers, investors, dealers, brokers, exchanges, custodians; buy-side vs sell-side; central banks' role in rates markets); coupon, principal, maturity, cash-flow schedules; par/premium/discount bonds; clean vs dirty price and accrued interest; yield vs price and why they move in opposite directions; trade date vs settlement date; security vs issuer vs exposure vs position; and the main market sectors (government/rates, IG credit, high yield, municipals, MBS, ABS, derivatives, EM debt). Running example: buy a corporate bond at a clean price of 102.25 — walk through coupon payments, principal repayment, accrued interest, dirty price, settlement cash, interest-rate exposure, credit exposure, and liquidity/funding considerations.

concepts.title: The Fixed-Income Product Family
concepts.brief: Introduce the major fixed-income instruments and the type of risk each represents. Cover: government securities (bills, notes, bonds, inflation-linked, on-the-run vs off-the-run, benchmark maturities); corporate bonds (IG, HY, seniority: senior unsecured/secured/subordinated, callable, putable, FRNs, convertibles, covenants); municipal bonds (GO vs revenue, tax treatment, call features); MBS (agency pass-throughs, pools, prepayments, extension/contraction risk, negative convexity); ABS (auto, credit-card, student-loan; tranches, credit enhancement, waterfalls); repo and reverse repo (secured borrowing/lending, GC vs special, haircuts, overnight/term/open, repo rates); interest-rate derivatives (swaps, SOFR, swaptions, Treasury futures and options, cheapest-to-deliver); credit derivatives (CDS premium/protection legs, default events, recovery, CDS-bond basis). Include a product map table: product → main exposure → typical business use → important risks.

concepts.title: From Mandate to Portfolio Position
concepts.brief: Explain how portfolio objectives become actual holdings, exposures, cash requirements, and risk positions. Cover: mandates, benchmarks, investment guidelines; accounts/portfolios/sleeves/strategies; long and short positions, net vs gross exposure; market value vs notional vs face value; position lots and tax lots; trade-date vs settlement-date positions; cash positions and projected cash flows; inventory management (dealer inventory vs investor holdings; available, borrowed, pledged, encumbered, financed inventory); aggregation by portfolio/issuer/sector/country/rating/currency/maturity bucket/duration bucket/risk factor. Walk the daily position lifecycle: start-of-day positions → orders → executions → allocations → amendments → settlements → coupon and principal events → financing → end-of-day positions → risk and P&L reporting. Distinguish realized vs unrealized P&L, mark-to-market, official books and records, and the front-office vs risk vs accounting vs custody vs regulatory views of a position. Optionally sketch the trade-lifecycle data model (Instrument, Order, RFQ, Execution, Allocation, Trade, PositionLot, Portfolio, Counterparty, Limit, etc.) and how a Portfolio and an Order relate to everything else.

concepts.title: Orders, Axes, and Execution
concepts.brief: Show how an investment decision becomes an executed fixed-income trade. Cover the order lifecycle: decision → pre-trade compliance/risk checks → order creation/approval/routing → RFQ → dealer quotes → execution decision → trade capture → allocation → confirmation → affirmation → settlement. Order types (market, limit, stop, relative-value, target-spread/yield, portfolio trades, list trading). Fixed-income market structure: quote-driven dealer markets, RFQ platforms, voice vs electronic, auctions, CLOBs, request-for-stream, all-to-all, portfolio trading. Pricing/liquidity language: bid, offer, mid, bid-ask spread, quote size, depth, executable vs indicative prices, market impact, slippage, information leakage. Axes: what an axis is, buy/sell axes, security-level vs sector vs curve vs risk-factor axes, strong vs weak, why traders use axes to find liquidity and improve execution quality. Execution history (timestamps, quotes, response times, venues, partial fills, amendments, rationale) and trader preferences (preferred dealers, counterparty rankings, minimum quotes, venues, protocols, ticket-size thresholds, restricted lists, auto-execution policies). Worked example: a PM buying $10 million of a corporate bond step by step from limit checks to settled position.

concepts.title: Counterparties, Credit, and Limits
concepts.brief: Explain the controls that determine who can trade, how much can be traded, and how risk is contained. Cover: the counterparty cast (dealers, banks, broker-dealers, asset managers, hedge funds, pensions, insurers, CCPs, custodians, tri-party agents, clearing members); counterparty structure (parent, legal entity, subsidiary, branch, fund, account, trading relationship, settlement entity); onboarding and legal docs (KYC, AML, tax docs, ISDA, CSA, GMRA, clearing/custody agreements, settlement instructions); counterparty risk flavors (pre-settlement, settlement, replacement-cost, wrong-way, concentration, country, legal, operational); the limit zoo (counterparty exposure, issuer, sector, country, rating, liquidity, concentration, duration, DV01, key-rate, CS01, spread-risk, stress-loss, trader authority, desk, portfolio); the control workflow (trade proposal → pre-trade limit check → compliance → eligibility → approval/warning → execution → post-trade exposure update → end-of-day monitoring); and limit governance (hard vs soft limits, warnings, overrides, escalations, approval workflows, audit trails, limit ownership and review).

concepts.title: Curves, Spreads, and Relative Value
concepts.brief: Teach the language used to compare bonds, derivatives, sectors, issuers, and maturities. Cover: yield curves (spot/zero, par, forward, discount factors; government/Treasury, swap, SOFR, credit curves; construction, interpolation, bootstrapping); curve trades (directional duration, steepeners, flatteners, butterflies, barbell vs bullet, key-rate trades, roll-down strategies); spread measures (nominal, G-spread, I-spread, asset-swap spread, Z-spread, OAS, credit spread, swap spread, spread-to-benchmark/curve); relative value (rich vs cheap, RV screens, peer and sector comparisons, historical spread percentiles, liquidity-adjusted RV); and basis (cash-futures, CDS-bond, swap spread, Treasury basis, funding basis, cross-currency; why basis persists: funding costs, collateral differences, liquidity, delivery options, dealer balance-sheet capacity, supply/demand, embedded optionality). Include example research statements like 'the 10-year point looks rich relative to the 7s and 30s' and 'this MBS sector offers attractive OAS but carries negative convexity', decoded into plain words.

concepts.title: Duration, DV01, Convexity, Carry, and Roll
concepts.brief: Explain the risk measures that turn market moves into estimated portfolio P&L. Cover: duration (Macaulay, modified, effective; duration as a first-order approximation; portfolio and benchmark-relative duration); DV01/PV01 (dollar value of a basis point, aggregating risk across instruments, net vs gross DV01, hedging DV01 with futures and swaps); key-rate durations (2y/5y/10y/30y key-rate DV01s, curve-shape risk, key-rate hedging); convexity (why duration alone is incomplete, positive vs negative convexity, callable bonds, MBS negative convexity, rate volatility); credit risk measures (credit spread, CS01, spread duration, credit beta, jump-to-default, recovery risk, migration risk); carry and roll (coupon carry, financing carry, pull-to-par, curve roll-down, spread roll, expected return from carry and roll, why carry is not free return, carry trades and tail risk); and the P&L attribution identity: total P&L = rates + spread + carry + roll + convexity + volatility + funding + FX + residual. Worked example: portfolio DV01 of $80,000, rates move +6bp, approximate rates P&L = -$480,000 — then discuss how convexity, spreads, carry, roll, and hedge effectiveness change the realized number.

concepts.title: Funding, Repo, Collateral, and Settlement
concepts.brief: Explain why financing and collateral are central to fixed-income trading, not operational afterthoughts. Cover: funding (why positions require funding, cash vs borrowed cash, leverage, funding cost and liquidity, balance-sheet constraints, internal transfer pricing); repo mechanics (repo and reverse repo structure, cash lent against collateral, overnight/term/open, GC vs special, repo rates, implied repo, fails and fails charges); collateral (eligibility, haircuts, initial vs variation margin, margin calls, excess collateral, substitutions, valuation, disputes, concentration, optimization); derivatives collateral (bilateral vs cleared, CCPs, IM/VM, CSAs); settlement (trade vs settlement date, DVP, custody, clearing, settlement instructions, fails, buy-ins, corporate actions); and funding stress (rising repo rates, haircut increases, collateral scarcity, margin calls, counterparty withdrawal, dealer balance-sheet constraints, liquidity spirals, forced deleveraging). Key lesson to land: a trade may look attractive on yield or spread but become unattractive after funding cost, haircuts, collateral requirements, and liquidity risk are included.

concepts.title: Liquidity, Market Data, Research, and Models
concepts.brief: Explain how desks build a market view, establish a price, and distinguish observable facts from model assumptions. Cover: liquidity (bid-ask spread, trade size, depth, immediacy, resiliency, dealer willingness to commit capital, transaction costs, liquid vs illiquid, benchmark vs off-the-run, liquidity in stress); market data in four families — reference data (identifiers, coupon, maturity, day-count, frequency, call schedules, conventions, rating, currency, sector), pricing data (dealer quotes, executed trades, composite and evaluated prices, closing/indicative prices, yields, spreads), market-risk data (curves, vol surfaces, prepayment assumptions, default probabilities, recovery assumptions), and event data (coupons, principal, calls, tenders, rating changes, defaults, macro announcements, central-bank decisions); data quality (stale prices, bad ticks, missing/sparse data, conflicting sources, timestamps, provenance, vendor differences, survivorship bias); research (macro, rates strategy, credit, sector, securitized, fundamental issuer, RV, quant; idea generation and the research-to-order workflow); models (cash-flow, discounting, curve construction, credit spread, Z-spread, OAS, prepayment, default probability, recovery, liquidity-cost, transaction-cost); and model governance (assumptions, calibration, validation, backtesting, benchmarking, versions, overrides, audit trail, explainability). Include the price-type distinction table: executed price vs dealer quote vs evaluated price vs composite price vs model price vs executable price.

concepts.title: A Day in the Life of a Fixed-Income Trade
concepts.brief: Connect the entire book through one end-to-end trade scenario. A portfolio manager expects intermediate Treasury yields to decline but believes corporate credit spreads may widen modestly; they want to buy an IG corporate bond, hedge part of the rate exposure, retain selected credit-spread exposure, finance the bond efficiently, and stay within portfolio, issuer, counterparty, and liquidity limits. Walk all ten steps: (1) form the thesis (macro outlook, rates and credit research, issuer selection, peer comparison on yield/spread/duration/CS01/carry/roll); (2) review the current portfolio (positions, cash, settlements, DV01, key-rate DV01, CS01, concentrations, liquidity, funding); (3) check constraints (guidelines, issuer/sector/rating/counterparty limits, trader authority, duration and stress-loss limits); (4) identify liquidity (axes, history, quotes, RFQ protocol, counterparties, size); (5) execute (order, RFQ, compare offers, quoted size, execution certainty, capture, allocate); (6) fund the position (cash need, repo financing, rate, haircut, collateral eligibility, funding cost in expected return); (7) hedge (bond DV01, futures vs swap, key-rate exposure, hedge sizing, basis risk); (8) monitor (revaluation, market data, spreads, rates, repo, collateral, counterparty exposure, limit utilization); (9) explain the P&L (rates, spread, carry, roll, convexity, hedge, funding, residual); (10) stress the trade (parallel shocks, steepening/flattening, spread widening, liquidity deterioration, funding-rate and haircut increases, counterparty downgrade, forced sale). This chapter should reference the ideas from every earlier chapter.

concepts.title: The Fixed-Income Math Primer
concepts.brief: A gentle appendix-style chapter that makes the arithmetic behind the whole book concrete, in plain words with small worked numbers: present value and future value, discount factors, yield-to-maturity, compounding conventions, day-count conventions, coupon calculations, accrued interest, clean vs dirty price, the price-yield relationship, duration, DV01, convexity, spread calculations, discount margin, Z-spread, and OAS. Keep it friendly — every formula gets a worked example with real numbers and a plain-word sentence saying what the number means. End with 'Questions for every trade' — the checklist a desk asks before approving any trade (thesis, which view, which risk type, carry and roll, DV01, CS01, funding, collateral, counterparties, limits, liquidity decline, repo rises, spreads widen, sharp yield moves, tomorrow's P&L explanation, execution evidence, data and model assumptions, unwind cost).

notes: Requested via issue form with a full syllabus ('Fixed Income in Practice — Markets, Trading, Risk, and the Life of a Bond Position'). Book promise: a practical introduction to fixed income as a business and operating system, following the full life of a trade (idea → portfolio decision → order/execution → position/settlement → funding/collateral → risk → P&L attribution → limits/controls), not just a list of securities or formulas. Editorial principle from the requester: every chapter should answer one operational question — what is held, why, how it is traded, how it is financed, how it is valued, what can make it lose money, and how the firm keeps the exposure within limits. The requester's Appendix B (product cheat sheets: Treasuries, corporates, munis, securitized, derivatives, funding products) and Appendix C (risk metric glossary: duration, DV01/PV01, key-rate DV01, convexity, CS01, carry, roll, Z-spread, OAS, basis, beta, haircut) should drive cheatsheet.html. The per-concept briefs above carry the requester's chapter-by-chapter topic lists.

images.prompt: A warm, ledger-paper illustration: ink-navy line art with a single brass-gold accent on cream paper, fine hand-ruled lines like an old trading-floor ledger, flat shapes, no gradients, no photographic detail. A schematic, not a picture. Subject: a long paper ribbon of coins and dated tickets unrolling across a table from one small figure to another, each ticket marked with a tiny calendar square — a stream of promised payments. No text labels baked in. Target size ~1280×720px, 16:9 landscape; compose for a small on-page figure with the subject centred and safe margins — it is letterboxed into a 16:9 box, so keep nothing important near the edges.
images.alt: A ribbon of coins and dated tickets unrolling from one figure to another
images.caption: A bond is a ribbon of promised payments.

designDirection: Trading Floor Ledger: warm cream ledger paper with faint ruled lines, ink-navy type in an old-style serif, sans small-caps for labels, one brass-gold accent, teal for links; flat, rational, no shadows beyond the spine.
